cards.q: State the conditions for simple harmonic motion.
cards.a: The acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position, and is always directed towards the equilibrium position (opposite to the displacement).

cards.q: Write the defining equation of simple harmonic motion, and say what the minus sign means.
cards.a: a=−ω2x\displaystyle a = -\omega^{2}xa=−ω2x. The minus sign shows that the acceleration is always in the opposite direction to the displacement: towards equilibrium.

cards.q: Write the condition for simple harmonic motion in terms of the resultant force on the oscillator.
cards.a: F=−kx\displaystyle F = -kxF=−kx: the restoring force is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.

cards.q: How does the period of a simple harmonic oscillator depend on its amplitude?
cards.a: It does not. The period is the same for any amplitude.
cards.why: A larger swing covers more distance but at a higher speed.

cards.q: The displacement of a simple harmonic oscillator is given by x=Acos⁡ωt\displaystyle x = A\cos\omega tx=Acosωt. Where is the oscillator at t=0\displaystyle t = 0t=0?
cards.a: At its maximum displacement, x=A\displaystyle x = Ax=A.
cards.why: cos⁡0=1\displaystyle \cos 0 = 1cos0=1. The equation describes an oscillation timed from the moment of release at the amplitude.

cards.a: 0.015 m

cards.q: Where in its motion does a simple harmonic oscillator have its maximum speed, and what is that speed?
cards.a: At the equilibrium position. Maximum speed =ωA\displaystyle = \omega A=ωA.

cards.q: Where in its motion does a simple harmonic oscillator have its maximum acceleration, and what is that acceleration?
cards.a: At maximum displacement. Maximum acceleration =ω2A\displaystyle = \omega^{2}A=ω2A.

cards.q: For an oscillator with displacement x=Acos⁡ωt\displaystyle x = A\cos\omega tx=Acosωt, write the equations for its velocity and its acceleration as functions of time.
cards.a: v=−Aωsin⁡ωt\displaystyle v = -A\omega\sin\omega tv=−Aωsinωt and a=−Aω2cos⁡ωt\displaystyle a = -A\omega^{2}\cos\omega ta=−Aω2cosωt.
cards.why: Each comes from the gradient of the graph before it: velocity from displacement, acceleration from velocity.

cards.q: For an oscillating object, what does the gradient of its displacement–time graph give, and the gradient of its velocity–time graph?
cards.a: Displacement–time: the velocity. Velocity–time: the acceleration.

cards.q: Describe how the velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs of a simple harmonic oscillator compare in phase with its displacement–time graph.
cards.a: The velocity is a quarter of a cycle (90°) out of phase with the displacement: it is greatest when the displacement is zero. The acceleration is in antiphase (180°) with the displacement.

cards.q: Write the equation for the period of a mass–spring system.
cards.a: T=2πmk\displaystyle T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}T=2πkm​​, where m\displaystyle mm is the mass and k\displaystyle kk the stiffness of the spring.

cards.a: 0.63 s

T=2π×0.10=0.63 s\displaystyle T = 2\pi \times 0.10 = 0.63\ \text{s}T=2π×0.10=0.63 s

cards.q: Write the equation for the period of a simple pendulum, and state the condition for it to hold.
cards.a: T=2πlg\displaystyle T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}T=2πgl​​, where l\displaystyle ll is the length of the pendulum. It holds only for small angles of swing.

cards.q: Which of these affect the period of a simple pendulum: its length, the mass of the bob, the gravitational field strength?
cards.a: Its length and the gravitational field strength. The mass of the bob does not.
cards.why: A mass–spring system is the other way round: its period depends on the mass but not on g\displaystyle gg.

cards.q: The mass on a spring is made four times larger. How does the period of oscillation change?
cards.a: It doubles.
cards.why: T∝m\displaystyle T \propto \sqrt{m}T∝m​, and 4=2\displaystyle \sqrt{4} = 24​=2.

cards.q: Why is the motion of a simple pendulum simple harmonic only for small angles?
cards.a: The restoring force is proportional to sin⁡θ\displaystyle \sin\thetasinθ. Only for small angles is sin⁡θ≈θ\displaystyle \sin\theta \approx \thetasinθ≈θ, which makes the restoring force proportional to the displacement.

cards.q: For an undamped simple harmonic oscillator, where is the kinetic energy greatest, where is the potential energy greatest, and what happens to the total?
cards.a: Kinetic energy is greatest at the equilibrium position. Potential energy is greatest at maximum displacement. The total energy stays constant.

cards.q: Describe the graphs of kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy against displacement for a simple harmonic oscillator.
cards.a: Potential energy: a U-shaped parabola, zero at the centre and greatest at ±A. Kinetic energy: an inverted parabola, greatest at the centre and zero at ±A. Total energy: a horizontal line.

cards.q: An oscillator has frequency f\displaystyle ff. At what frequency do its kinetic energy and its potential energy vary with time?
cards.a: At 2f\displaystyle 2f2f: each rises and falls twice in every oscillation.
cards.why: The oscillator passes through equilibrium, where kinetic energy peaks, twice per cycle.

cards.a: 0.025 J

E=12×0.20×0.502=0.025 J\displaystyle E = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.20 \times 0.50^{2} = 0.025\ \text{J}E=21​×0.20×0.502=0.025 J

cards.q: What is damping?
cards.a: The removal of energy from an oscillating system by resistive forces, such as friction or air resistance, so that its amplitude decreases.

cards.q: Describe the effect of light damping on the amplitude and the period of an oscillation.
cards.a: The amplitude decreases gradually with each oscillation. The period stays almost the same.

cards.q: How does the plastic deformation of a ductile material reduce the amplitude of an oscillation?
cards.a: Work done in deforming the material plastically is not returned to the oscillator: the energy is dissipated. With less energy in the oscillation, its amplitude falls.

cards.q: What is the difference between a free oscillation and a forced oscillation?
cards.a: In a free oscillation the system is displaced and left to oscillate at its own natural frequency. In a forced oscillation a periodic driving force makes the system oscillate at the frequency of the driver.

cards.q: What is the natural frequency of a system?
cards.a: The frequency at which it oscillates freely, with no driving force acting.

cards.q: What is resonance?
cards.a: When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system, the amplitude of oscillation is a maximum: energy is transferred from the driver most efficiently.
cards.why: Both parts are needed: the frequency condition and the maximum amplitude.

cards.q: Describe the graph of amplitude against driving frequency for a lightly damped system.
cards.a: The amplitude is small at low and at high driving frequencies and rises to a sharp peak at the natural frequency.

cards.q: How does increasing the damping change the resonance curve of a system?
cards.a: The peak is lower and broader (less sharp), and it moves to a slightly lower frequency.

cards.q: Give one example of resonance in a mechanical system, and one involving stationary waves.
cards.a: Mechanical: a bridge or building set oscillating by wind or footsteps at its natural frequency. Stationary waves: a stretched string driven at one of its harmonic frequencies, which sets up a large stationary wave.

cards.q: A student writes: "Resonance happens when the natural frequency is increased to its maximum." Correct this.
cards.a: The natural frequency is a fixed property of the system. Resonance happens when the driving frequency is adjusted until it equals the natural frequency; it is the amplitude that reaches a maximum.

cards.q: Outline how to use a simple pendulum to find a value for g\displaystyle gg.
cards.a: Measure the period for several lengths and plot T2\displaystyle T^{2}T2 against l\displaystyle ll.
marks: Measure the length l\displaystyle ll from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob.
Release the pendulum from a small angle and time at least 10 oscillations; divide to find the period T\displaystyle TT.
Use a fiducial marker at the equilibrium position to judge the start and end of the timing.
Repeat for a range of lengths.
Plot T2\displaystyle T^{2}T2 against l\displaystyle ll: a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π2g\displaystyle \frac{4\pi^{2}}{g}g4π2​.

cards.q: When timing oscillations, why is the fiducial marker placed at the equilibrium position and not at the end of the swing?
cards.a: The oscillator moves fastest through the equilibrium position, so the moment it passes the marker can be judged most precisely. At the end of the swing it is momentarily at rest, and the moment is hard to judge.

cards.q: Outline how to determine an unknown mass using the resonant frequencies of known masses on a spring.
cards.a: Find the resonant frequency for each known mass, plot a calibration graph, and read the unknown mass from it.
marks: Hang a known mass on a spring attached to a vibration generator driven by a signal generator.
Adjust the driving frequency until the amplitude of oscillation is a maximum, and record this resonant frequency.
Repeat for a range of known masses.
Plot 1f2\displaystyle \frac{1}{f^{2}}f21​ against mass: a straight line.
Find the resonant frequency for the unknown mass and read its mass from the graph.
